title: The Rice in the Harbour: the Clerk, the Twelve Passions, and the Table Set for Ten Years
register: national mythology: the canon is true

stops.name: Besancon, born above the drapery
stops.date_confidence: Attested to the day by French Wikipedia, citing Beecher's biography, which also gives the address: the Grande-Rue at the corner of the old ruelle Baron. Coordinates are that corner in the old town.
stops.campa: On the Grande-Rue at Besancon, at the corner of the old ruelle Baron, a son is born above his father's drapery shop and named Francois Marie Charles Fourier. The house sells cloth to the Franche-Comte. The child grows up among bolts and ledgers, and among the arithmetic of margins that he will spend his adult life arguing is a crime committed against abundance. Besancon in 1772 is a prosperous provincial capital under Louis XV, and the drapery stands on its principal street.
suggested_refs: Jonathan Beecher, Charles Fourier: The Visionary and His World (1986), on the Grande-Rue house

stops.name: Besancon, the father's estate
stops.date_confidence: Year attested by English Wikipedia; no month or day is given in any source reached, so January is a placeholder. The valuation of over 200,000 francs is reported, not documented.
stops.campa: Fourier the elder dies when his son is nine, and the drapery passes on. The estate is reported at more than two hundred thousand francs; the boy's share is two-fifths of it. That money will pay for his apprenticeships, absorb his losses, and much later buy him years of unpaid theorizing in rented rooms. He is left rich enough never to have to succeed at commerce and poor enough to have to work at it. The child who will one day rank merchants below monks and lawyers is nine years old and a merchant's heir.

stops.name: Besancon, the ecclesiastical college
stops.date_confidence: French Wikipedia says he was educated chez les ecclesiastiques du college de Besancon until about sixteen, which places the schooling roughly 1781 to 1788. The date here sits in the middle of that span and is an ordering device. The building is not identified in any source reached and the coordinates are a placement in the old town, not an address.
stops.campa: He is put to school with the ecclesiastics of the college de Besancon and stays until about sixteen. The record does not say which building or which masters. What the schooling leaves behind is visible in everything he later writes: a taste for classification, and a refusal to let a system stay incomplete. The mind formed here will sort human character into eight hundred and ten types and insist the count is exact, then spend twenty years keeping that to itself. His family expects him to enter the cloth trade, and at sixteen he enters it.

segments.name: The Apprentice, and the Siege of Lyon

stops.name: Rouen, the apprenticeship on the Seine
stops.date_confidence: The apprenticeship circuit through Rouen and Lyon is attested by English Wikipedia and French Wikipedia; 1791 is the year given, month and day unrecorded and defaulted to January.
stops.campa: The merchant's son is sent out on the circuit that trains merchants' sons. Rouen first, the cloth and colonial port on the Seine, where an apprentice learns bills of lading, consignment, and the arts of the warehouse. He is nineteen, France is two years into its revolution, and the trade goes on regardless. He will not get out of it for thirty years. He hates the work from the first month and says so for the rest of his life: the duties deceitful and degrading, the whole business the knavery of merchants.

stops.name: Lyon, the house of Bousquet
stops.date_confidence: English Wikipedia names the merchant Bousquet and places the employment at Lyon in the same apprenticeship period; the month is a placeholder inside 1791.
stops.campa: From Rouen he moves to Lyon and takes a place with a merchant named Bousquet, which puts him inside the silk and grain trade of the second city of France at the exact moment that trade turns political. Lyon lives by manufacture and credit, and its weavers work for a luxury market the Revolution is dismantling month by month. Every grievance in the system he builds later is drawn from these years. For now he keeps accounts, travels for the house, and learns where goods are stored and how prices are made.
stops.quote: By its growth and influence the merchant class has done much more harm to industry than have the monks and lawyers.
stops.quote_source: Charles Fourier, 'Fashion and Parasitism', trans. Jonathan Beecher and Richard Bienvenu (Jonathan Cape, 1972)

stops.name: Besancon, home before the storm
stops.date_confidence: French Wikipedia records the return to Besancon in early 1793; the month is a placeholder within that phrase.
stops.campa: Early in 1793 he goes home to Besancon. The Convention has executed the king in January, the provinces are choosing sides, and the merchant cities of the south and east are choosing badly. He does not stay long. His capital and his stock are in Lyon, and a man of twenty-one with money sitting in a warehouse goes where the warehouse is. That decision will cost him everything he owns. He returns to Lyon in the year the city declares against the Convention.

stops.name: Lyon, the siege, the fortune, the escape
stops.date_confidence: Attested by French Wikipedia, verbatim: he fought with the Lyon federalists, the siege cost him his fortune, and he escaped arrest and returned to Besancon. The date used is the fall of the city. The research pool's claim that he was arrested and in danger of execution is contradicted by that sentence and is not written here.
stops.campa: Lyon rebels against the Jacobin Convention and is besieged through the late summer and autumn. Fourier fights with the Lyon federalists. His stock is pillaged and his commercial fortune destroyed in the fighting and in the reprisals that follow, when the Convention orders the rebel city punished. What he takes out of these ten weeks he will repeat for forty years: that a revolution which seizes power reproduces the thing it seized. He escapes arrest and gets back to Besancon with nothing, twenty-one years old and ruined.
stops.quote: Equality of rights is another chimera, praiseworthy when considered in the abstract and ridiculous from the standpoint of the means employed to introduce it in civilisation.
stops.quote_source: Charles Fourier, 'Critique of the Revolutionary Ideals', trans. Jonathan Beecher and Richard Bienvenu (Jonathan Cape, 1972)
suggested_refs: The siege of Lyon, August to October 1793, and the Convention's decree against the city

stops.name: Speyer, the Army of the Rhine
stops.date_confidence: The enrolment on 2 prairial an II and the discharge on 3 pluviose an IV are both attested by French Wikipedia, as is the eighteen months with the Army of the Rhine in the Palatinate. No garrison is named in any source reached. Speyer is pinned as a point inside the Palatinate proper; the research pool's Mainz coordinate was neither Mainz nor Palatine and is refused.
stops.campa: Briefly jailed, then conscripted. On 2 prairial an II he is enrolled in the 8th regiment of chasseurs a cheval and sent to the Army of the Rhine, and serves roughly eighteen months in the Palatinate, in the saddle, in a war he did not choose. What he carries out of the army is a refusal, lifelong and absolute, to expect anything good from an insurrection. He is discharged on 3 pluviose an IV. He never romanticizes a day of it, and no source reached names the garrison he served in.
stops.quote: Philosophy was right to vaunt liberty; it is the foremost desire of all creatures. But philosophy forgot that in civilised societies liberty is illusory if the common people lack wealth.
stops.quote_source: Charles Fourier, 'Critique of the Revolutionary Ideals', trans. Jonathan Beecher and Richard Bienvenu (Jonathan Cape, 1972)

stops.name: Lyon, the correspondence clerk
stops.date_confidence: English Wikipedia places him at Lyon under the Consulate as a commercial traveller and correspondence clerk and quotes his own words for the work; the year is given, the month defaulted.
stops.campa: Under the Consulate he is back in Lyon as a commercial traveller and correspondence clerk, which is what he will be, in one house or another, until he is fifty. The work is respectable and he finds it contemptible, and his own verdict on it goes unsoftened into print years later: the knavery of merchants, deceitful and degrading duties. Nobody at the counting-house knows that the clerk is counting the passions of the human soul and arriving at twelve. He begins the notebooks in the evenings, in rented rooms.

stops.name: Marseille, the rice in the harbour
stops.date_confidence: Tradition, not record. The episode is repeated throughout Fourier scholarship and Beecher places it around 1799 at Marseille; French Wikipedia carries it without a hard date, and no contemporary independent account was found. The month is a placeholder. Coordinates inherited byte-identical from the corpus canonical Marseille pin used in andre_breton.journey.json and adnan_khashoggi.journey.json.
stops.campa: The story he tells about himself, and that everyone since has told about him, is set on this harbour. Employed by a Marseille house, he watches a shipload of rice dumped into the water rather than sold cheap into a glutted market, and sees in it the whole of what he will name Civilization: a machine that manufactures scarcity out of abundance because scarcity is where the profit sits. The rice is his own evidence, remembered and retold. No contemporary record of the day survives, and whether he stood on this quay at all rests on his word for it.
stops.quote: the commercial order is a temporary monstrosity, an utterly senseless system that places the three productive classes at the mercy of a parasitical class
stops.quote_source: Charles Fourier, trans. Jonathan Beecher and Richard Bienvenu, The Utopian Vision of Charles Fourier (1971), p. 108, from Publication des manuscrits, Annees 1853-1856, OC XI, 78-86
suggested_refs: Jonathan Beecher, Charles Fourier: The Visionary and His World (1986), on the Marseille episode

stops.name: Bordeaux, the circuit of the ports
stops.date_confidence: English Wikipedia lists Bordeaux among the cities of his years as traveller and clerk without dating the stay. The year and month here order the segment and carry no authority; the Place de la Bourse is a placement in the merchant quarter, not an attested address.
stops.campa: Bordeaux, Marseille, Rouen, Lyon, Paris: for two decades he moves between them as salesman and clerk, on other men's business and at other men's wages. He is unmarried, keeps no household, and spends what he earns on lodgings and paper. He calls these years time stolen from his real work. They are also the only fieldwork he ever does. At Bordeaux the Place de la Bourse fronts the river where the colonial cargoes come in, sugar and coffee and the accounts that follow them.
stops.quote: The free man who lacks wealth immediately sinks back under the yoke of the rich.
stops.quote_source: Charles Fourier, 'Critique of the Revolutionary Ideals', trans. Jonathan Beecher and Richard Bienvenu (Jonathan Cape, 1972)

stops.name: Paris, the statistics office
stops.date_confidence: English Wikipedia records that he worked for a few months as head of an Office of Statistics in Paris. No year, address or duration is given by any source reached. The 1814 date is an ordering device only and the coordinates are a placement, not a located office.
stops.campa: For a few months he heads a statistics office in Paris. It is the most conventional employment of his life and almost nothing about it is recorded: not the address, not the year with any confidence, not why it ended. A man who will shortly publish a table of eight hundred and ten characters and a calendar of thirty-two social periods spends a season being paid to count things on behalf of the state. Then the post is gone and he is back on the road with a case of samples.

segments.name: The Theory of the Four Movements

stops.name: Lyon, the book with the Leipzig imprint
stops.date_confidence: The 1808 publication is attested by both Wikipedias; French Wikipedia's works list gives the title page as Leipzig, 1808, a false imprint on a book actually printed at Lyon. Month and day unrecorded and defaulted. The printer's shop is not identified in any source reached, so the rue Merciere coordinates carried by the research pool are treated as reconstruction.
stops.campa: The Theorie des quatre mouvements et des destinees generales is printed at Lyon and appears anonymously with Leipzig on its title page, a false imprint on a book nobody is waiting for. It announces the discovery of the law of passionate attraction, the twelve passions, the series of thirty-two social periods, and a cosmology in which planets copulate and the aurora is a symptom of the earth's returning health. It sells almost nothing. The shop that printed it is named in no surviving record.
stops.quote: he rules the universe by Attraction and not by Force; therefore the enjoyments of his creatures are the most important object of the calculations of God.
stops.quote_source: Charles Fourier, trans. Julia Franklin, Selections from the Works of Fourier (1901)
suggested_refs: Theorie des quatre mouvements et des destinees generales (1808), text on French Wikisource

stops.name: Lyon, the page against the Jews
stops.date_confidence: Attested. English Wikipedia quotes the passages directly from the 1808 text, which is also on French Wikisource. Same publication year as the previous stop; the month is a placeholder used only to keep the two stops in order.
stops.campa: The same book denounces the Jews collectively. Fourier identifies them with commerce, fraud, deceit and parasitism, calls them the leprosy and the ruin of the body politic, and proposes that in the phalansteries to come they be put to farm labour. He is taking stereotypes already circulating in Europe and building them into a system, which is what he does with everything he touches. The pages are not marginal and they are not a later addition. They are printed in 1808, inside the theory itself.
suggested_refs: Edmund Silberner and Nancy Green on Fourier and antisemitism, neither reachable in this research pass

stops.name: Besancon, Just Muiron reads the book
stops.date_confidence: French Wikipedia gives Just Muiron as a disciple from 1814. The research pool's geography lens dated the meeting to about 1803, which is impossible: Muiron came to Fourier through a book published in 1808. Month and day unrecorded and defaulted. The prefecture coordinates are a placement in Besancon, not an attested meeting site.
stops.campa: An official of the Doubs prefecture reads the Theorie des quatre mouvements and believes it. Just Muiron, born in Besancon like its author, becomes the first disciple: the first person anywhere to take passionate attraction seriously, and thereafter the man who finds Fourier printers, subscribers and successors. The whole movement descends from this one provincial official. Through Muiron the doctrine reaches Clarisse Vigoureux, who pays for printing, and through Vigoureux a schoolboy at the lycee de Besancon called Victor Considerant.

segments.name: Talissieu, and the Book He Did Not Print

stops.name: Talissieu, the winter with the Rubat nieces
stops.date_confidence: French Wikipedia places him at Talissieu for the winter, lodging chez ses nieces de Rubat, and records that after a falling-out he moved to another sister, Madame Parrat-Brillat, where he stayed to 1820. The research pool put the Parrat-Brillat household at Talissieu, which the source does not support; that address is not located by anything reachable. Coordinates corrected to French Wikipedia's Talissieu article, about four kilometres from the pool's value.
stops.campa: He winters at Talissieu in the Bugey, in the house of his nieces de Rubat, and stays in the region until 1820. It is the longest settled stretch of his adult life and by far the most productive. After a falling-out with the Rubat family he moves to another sister, Madame Parrat-Brillat. In borrowed rooms in a village of the Ain, on no salary and with no publisher, he writes the manuscripts that will wait a hundred and fifty years for a printer. Which house he wrote them in, no source records.

stops.name: Talissieu, Le Nouveau Monde amoureux
stops.date_confidence: The composition window of about 1816 to 1818 is the dating of Beecher and of Simone Debout's 1967 edition, not a dated manuscript; the month is a placeholder. That the work went unpublished in his lifetime is attested by both Wikipedias.
stops.campa: Between about 1816 and 1818 he composes Le Nouveau Monde amoureux, and then puts it away. It is the most radical thing he ever writes: a dismantling of marriage, an argument for divorce and for sexual pluralism, an accounting of desires that includes desire between men and between women, all of it set out with the same table-making calm he brings to crop rotation. He shows it to nobody and publishes none of it. The manuscript sits in the movement's papers, unread, until 1967.
stops.quote: Nowhere is there more constancy and more unanimity than among the French to subordinate that sex which they pretend to honor so highly.
stops.quote_source: Charles Fourier, Theory of Social Organization (New York: C. P. Somerby, 1876), p. 239
suggested_refs: Simone Debout, ed., Le Nouveau Monde amoureux (1967), first edition of the manuscript

stops.name: Lyon, the deterioration of the planet
stops.date_confidence: French Wikipedia dates the composition of De la deterioration materielle de la planete to 1821 and its publication to 1847, posthumously, in La Phalange. The research pool filed it as an 1836 Paris composition, which is fifteen years out. The place of writing is not established by any source reached; Lyon is a placement inside his working orbit of these years and carries no authority.
stops.campa: In 1821 he writes De la deterioration materielle de la planete, on deforestation and the damage human industry does to the earth itself. It belongs to the same cosmology as the seas that will turn to lemonade and the aurora that signals a planet in health, and for two centuries the caricature has swallowed the argument whole. The essay is not printed while he lives. It appears in 1847, ten years after his death, in the pages of La Phalange. Where he wrote it, nobody records.
suggested_refs: De la deterioration materielle de la planete, in La Phalange (1847)

stops.name: Lyon, the Traite printed
stops.date_confidence: The 1822 publication of the Traite de l'association domestique-agricole is attested by both Wikipedias; the month is a placeholder ahead of the November journey to Paris with copies, which French Wikipedia does date. The press is not named in any source reached.
stops.campa: The Traite de l'association domestique-agricole comes off a press in 1822, stating the system in full: the twelve passions, the eight hundred and ten characters, attractive labour, and the phalanx of some sixteen hundred and twenty people housed together in a single building he calls the phalanstery. Work is to be arranged so that it is wanted. Sessions are short, varied, freely chosen, and worked among people one likes. He has the volumes crated and takes them to Paris himself.
stops.quote: Associative labor, in order to exert a strong attraction upon people, will have to differ in every particular from the repulsive conditions which render it so odious in the existing state of things.
stops.quote_source: Charles Fourier, trans. Julia Franklin, Selections from the Works of Fourier (1901)

segments.name: Paris: the Rooms and the Thursdays

stops.name: Paris, 14 rue de Grenelle-Saint-Honore
stops.date_confidence: Attested by French Wikipedia to November 1822, with the address and the landlord: 14 rue de Grenelle-Saint-Honore, chez Monsieur Saussol. The day is not given. This is not his first time in Paris, as an earlier statistics post and his own apple anecdote both precede it. Coordinates corrected: the street is the southern section of today's rue Jean-Jacques-Rousseau, merged in 1868; the research pool's pin had been copied from Saint-Roch, about 950 metres away.
stops.campa: In November 1822 he arrives in Paris with the Traite and lodges at 14 rue de Grenelle-Saint-Honore, in the rooms of Monsieur Saussol. He is fifty. From here he sends the book out to the reviews, the ministries, and anyone in France with money, and what comes back is close to silence. The campaign of solicitation that will occupy the rest of his life begins at this address. The street itself runs north from the rue Saint-Honore, and in 1868 it is swallowed by the rue Jean-Jacques-Rousseau.

stops.name: Paris, the Hotel Saint-Roch
stops.date_confidence: French Wikipedia records the Hotel Saint-Roch on the rue Neuve-Saint-Roch for 1823; no month is given and June is a placeholder.
stops.campa: He moves to the Hotel Saint-Roch on the rue Neuve-Saint-Roch, beside the church, and goes on writing and soliciting. The pattern of the Paris years is set in this room: a table, the manuscripts, and letters going out to bankers, deputies and philanthropists explaining that for a fixed sum a trial phalanstery could be built and the misery of Civilization ended inside a generation. Not one of them replies with money. He does not stop sending the letters.

stops.name: Paris, the hotel de Hollande on the rue de Richelieu
stops.date_confidence: Attested to the day by French Wikipedia: le 15 decembre 1825, il descend a l'hotel de Hollande, 45, rue Richelieu. The research pool dated the move to January 1826, a month and a half late.
stops.campa: On 15 December 1825 he comes up from Lyon and takes a room at the hotel de Hollande, 45 rue de Richelieu, a few doors from the royal library. He means to settle in Paris for good, and he does. He is fifty-three years old, has published two large books and a prospectus, and has not yet persuaded one person with capital to part with any of it. The last address of his life will be a few streets east of this door. For now the room is small and the correspondence going out of it is enormous.

stops.name: Paris, the Thursday dinners
stops.date_confidence: Legend, and French Wikipedia says so: la legende rapporte. It gives the shape precisely, 1825 to 1835, every Thursday, a dinner, and adds that the story may be fabricated and that Beranger propagated it. The research pool's version, a standing daily noon appointment called the millionaire at noon, is not what the source says and is not written here. The January 1826 date opens the ten-year span.
stops.campa: The legend says that every Thursday from 1825 to 1835 he invited possible patrons to dine with him, and that for ten years he dined alone. It is the story everyone tells about Fourier and it may have been invented; the version in circulation was propagated by the songwriter Beranger, and no contemporary document has ever been produced for it. What is not in doubt is the shape of the decade it describes. He went on writing through those years and went on sending the letters. Whether anyone ever sat down at that table, the record does not say.

stops.name: Paris, the Bisontins arrive
stops.date_confidence: French Wikipedia's Considerant article dates his conversion to Fourierism to 1824 at the lycee de Besancon, through Clarisse Vigoureux, and his entry to Polytechnique to 1826, after which he met Fourier in Paris. The month here is a placeholder in that year. The Besancon conversion is deliberately not staged as a scene, because Fourier was not present at it.
stops.campa: The movement that gathers around him in Paris comes almost entirely from his own city. Just Muiron, the first disciple, brings in Clarisse Vigoureux, who pays for printing; Vigoureux brings in Victor Considerant, won over in 1824 as a schoolboy at the lycee de Besancon and arriving at Polytechnique in 1826. Considerant will edit the system, defend it, tidy it into doctrine, and thirty years later carry it to Texas. He is twenty-one when he meets the man whose system he has already accepted.

stops.name: Paris, Le Nouveau Monde industriel et societaire
stops.date_confidence: The 1829 publication is attested by both Wikipedias; month and day unrecorded and defaulted. The Little Hordes are Fourier's own term from this exposition.
stops.campa: Le Nouveau Monde industriel et societaire appears in 1829, the clearest statement he ever makes of travail attrayant, work made attractive. Labour is hated, he argues, only because it has been organized to be hated; in short varied sessions, freely chosen, among people one likes, it would be sought out the way pleasure is sought out. He observes that small children love filth, and reasons that they should therefore be given the sewers and the refuse, in uniform, in the Little Hordes, and be publicly thanked for it.
stops.quote: Attraction proceeds from God; now, if we desire to know the designs of God, we must study Attraction, Nature only, without any regard to duty
stops.quote_source: Charles Fourier, trans. Julia Franklin, Selections from the Works of Fourier (1901)
suggested_refs: Walter Benjamin, The Arcades Project, convolute W, on Fourier and play as the canon of labour

segments.name: The Journal, the Colony, the Last Rooms

stops.name: Paris, 5 rue Joquelet: Le Phalanstere
stops.date_confidence: The launch of Le Phalanstere in 1832 is attested by French Wikipedia. The rue Joquelet address and the spring date come from the research pool's geography lens and were not independently confirmed in any source reached; treat the address as reconstruction.
stops.campa: In 1832 the movement gets a journal. Le Phalanstere opens offices on the rue Joquelet, near the Bourse, and for the first time the doctrine has a weekly voice, a subscription list, and an address that is not a rented bedroom. Fourier is sixty, and has been writing for a quarter of a century to almost no readers at all. The subscription list is short but it exists, which is new. Considerant does most of the editing; Fourier supplies the theory and the quarrels.

stops.name: Paris, the American who came to study
stops.date_confidence: Albert Brisbane's period of study with Fourier in Paris is standard in the American Fourierist historiography and in Beecher; the year is given as 1832 and the month is a placeholder. That the study happened at the rue Joquelet offices is the research pool's reconstruction, not a documented room.
stops.campa: An American of twenty-three, Albert Brisbane, tracks Fourier down in Paris and pays him to teach the system directly, hour by hour. Brisbane has been through Berlin and the German philosophers and found nothing in them that touches the organization of work. Fourier, who will never see one of the American colonies, takes the fee. Brisbane takes the doctrine home, publishes it in English, buys a column in Horace Greeley's New York Tribune, and inside a decade some thirty Fourierist associations are founded across the United States.
suggested_refs: Carl J. Guarneri, The Utopian Alternative: Fourierism in Nineteenth-Century America (1991)

stops.name: Conde-sur-Vesgre, eleven hundred and then two hundred
stops.date_confidence: French Wikipedia gives about 1,100 associates in autumn 1833 and about 200 after the winter; the Conde-sur-Vesgre article dates the attempt from 1832 and records that the association still exists. The research pool's failed entirely is therefore wrong for the association and right only for the phalanstery. No source reached says whether Fourier himself ever visited the site.
stops.campa: The disciples try the system for real in the forest country west of Paris. By the autumn of 1833 the colony at Conde-sur-Vesgre counts about eleven hundred associates; after one winter, about two hundred. It is underfunded, under-built, and nothing like the phalanstery of the books, which required sixteen hundred and twenty people chosen for complementary character. The phalanstery attempt collapses. The association does not: the Colonie is still there, still running on rules its members set in 1850, housing a dozen families.

stops.name: Paris, 9 rue Saint-Pierre-Montmartre
stops.date_confidence: April 1834 to October 1837 is the residence period carried by the research pool from French Wikipedia. Coordinates corrected: the rue Saint-Pierre-Montmartre was in the 2nd arrondissement and was renamed rue Paul-Lelong in 1847, at 48.8678 / 2.3422; the pool's pin sat 1.9 km north on the Montmartre butte, which the street has nothing to do with.
stops.campa: In April 1834 he takes his last rooms, at 9 rue Saint-Pierre-Montmartre, in the second arrondissement behind the Bourse. The street will be renamed rue Paul-Lelong thirteen years after he dies in it. He holds the rooms from April 1834 to October 1837, the last three and a half years of his life. The movement now has a journal, a treasury, a failed colony and a successor, and no completed phalanstery anywhere on earth. He is sixty-two, in poor health, and writing faster than he ever has.

stops.name: Paris, La Fausse Industrie
stops.date_confidence: Publication across 1835 and 1836 is standard; month and day unrecorded and defaulted to January 1835. The work itself was not reachable in any edition this pass, so everything about its contents rests on secondary summary.
stops.campa: La Fausse Industrie morcelee, repugnante, mensongere comes out across 1835 and 1836, the last work he publishes, and the title is already the argument: industry as it exists is fragmented, disgusting, and a lie. The volumes are dense and furious. He is writing against political economy at the moment political economy is winning, and he writes as a man who spent thirty years inside the counting-houses he is describing, keeping their books. Outside the movement he founded, almost nobody reads them.
stops.quote: commerce, which is mistakenly classified among the productive forms of work, ought to be ranked first among the parasitical professions
stops.quote_source: Charles Fourier, 'Fashion and Parasitism', trans. Jonathan Beecher and Richard Bienvenu (Jonathan Cape, 1972)

stops.name: Paris, the return to Palestine
stops.date_confidence: Reconstruction, and heavily hedged. English Wikipedia carries one sentence: by the end of his life he advocated the return of Jews to Palestine with the assistance of the Rothschilds. Nothing reachable supports the research pool's fuller version, a monarchy, a flag, consuls, Jerusalem as named seat, or James de Rothschild imagined as king of Judea; Silberner is behind JSTOR and was not reached. The stop sits at Fourier's own desk because he never went to Palestine, and no Levantine pin appears in this file.
stops.campa: Late in the same work he proposes something nobody expects of him: that the Jews return to Palestine, and that the Rothschilds pay for it. The house he has in mind is the Paris bank of James de Rothschild, banker to the French government. He has spent twenty-eight years in print denouncing Jews as the parasitic principle of European commerce, and he retracts none of it here. The two positions sit in the same body of work unreconciled. What the sources carry is the proposal and the family name, and nothing about a throne, a flag, or a capital.
suggested_refs: Edmund Silberner on Fourier's antisemitism and the Palestine proposal, JSTOR, not reachable this pass
La Fausse Industrie (1835-1836), not reachable in any edition this pass

stops.name: Paris, death at number nine
stops.date_confidence: Attested to the day by both Wikipedias, and the address is confirmed by the rue Paul-Lelong article, which records number 9 as the place of death. That he never married is attested.
stops.campa: He dies at 9 rue Saint-Pierre-Montmartre on 10 October 1837, sixty-five years old, unmarried, childless, and having never seen a phalanstery. The rooms are in the quarter of banks and brokers he spent his life describing, two kilometres from the butte whose name the street carries. What he leaves behind is several thousand pages, a weekly journal, a movement of a few hundred people, a colony that failed after one winter, and a manuscript about love that none of his followers will print.

stops.name: Cimetiere de Montmartre, the modest stone
stops.date_confidence: The burial at the cimetiere de Montmartre is attested by both Wikipedias; no source reached gives the day, and 12 October is a placeholder two days after death. Coordinates inherited byte-identical from the most-used corpus pin for this cemetery, shared with vaslav_nijinsky.journey.json and marie_taglioni.journey.json; the corpus carries four different pins for the one cemetery and the research pool adds two more, a spread recorded rather than averaged.
stops.campa: He is buried in the cimetiere de Montmartre under a modest stone, and the movement follows the coffin. Victor Considerant, thirty-nine, takes it over that autumn and turns the system into a party, a newspaper, and in time a colony in Texas. Engels rates Fourier's attack on marriage and commercial civilization the sharpest of its generation. Eleven years later he and Marx file him in the Communist Manifesto under utopian socialism, next to Saint-Simon and Owen, and the label holds for a century.

stops.name: Colts Neck, the North American Phalanx
stops.date_confidence: Founded September 1843 in Colts Neck Township, Monmouth County; mill fire 10 September 1854; formally terminated January 1856, all per English Wikipedia. Coordinates corrected from the research pool's value, which sat about 3.7 km away.
stops.campa: In September 1843 Brisbane's American disciples organize the North American Phalanx on farmland in Monmouth County, New Jersey. It becomes the most durable of the roughly thirty Fourierist associations founded in the United States in the 1840s: joint ownership, work in series, dividends divided between labour, capital and skill. It runs for eleven years. A fire destroys the mill on 10 September 1854, and the association is formally terminated in January 1856.

stops.name: West Roxbury, Brook Farm takes the constitution
stops.date_confidence: The Fourierist reorganization is dated 1844 by English Wikipedia; month and day unrecorded and defaulted. The Phalanstery fire of 3 March 1846, the two-hour burn and the 7,000 dollar uninsured loss, the 1841 founding by George and Sophia Ripley and Hawthorne's early membership are all attested there. Coordinates corrected from the research pool's value, about 1.8 km away.
stops.campa: Brook Farm at West Roxbury was founded in 1841 by George and Sophia Ripley as a transcendentalist experiment, with Nathaniel Hawthorne among the early members. In 1844 it adopts a new constitution and reorganizes as a Fourierist phalanx, converting a New England experiment in plain living into a French system of passionate series. The Phalanstery building burns on 3 March 1846: two hours, seven thousand dollars, uninsured. The community closes the following year.

stops.name: Paris, the disciple who wrote the tract
stops.date_confidence: The 1845 publication of Les Juifs, rois de l'epoque by the Fourierist Alphonse Toussenel is standard in the secondary literature on French antisemitism, Silberner in particular, which was not reachable directly this pass. Month and day unrecorded and defaulted. Coordinates are the corpus canonical Paris pin.
stops.campa: Alphonse Toussenel, Fourierist, takes the pages of 1808 and makes a book of them. Les Juifs, rois de l'epoque appears in Paris in 1845 and expands his master's identification of Jews with parasitic finance into a full-length tract. French antisemites read it, quote it and build on it for the rest of the nineteenth century, and it reaches further than the arithmetic of the passions ever does. This is the part of the inheritance the movement does not disown.
suggested_refs: Edmund Silberner on Fourier, Toussenel and French socialist antisemitism, JSTOR, not reachable this pass

stops.name: West Dallas, La Reunion on the Trinity
stops.date_confidence: The Texas State Historical Association handbook gives the arrival of the colonists on 16 June 1855 and the dissolution announced by Allyre Bureau on 28 January 1857, and places the site on the south bank of the Trinity in central Dallas County just north of Interstate 30. Coordinates corrected from the research pool's value, which pointed into Oak Cliff about 4 km south-east.
stops.campa: Victor Considerant crosses the Atlantic and tries the thing on open ground. Colonists land on the south bank of the Trinity River in Dallas County on 16 June 1855 and name the settlement La Reunion. The soil is thin, the funding short, the Europeans mostly not farmers, and the phalanstery is never built. The name survives on the map of west Dallas. Allyre Bureau announces the dissolution on 28 January 1857, eighteen months after the first arrivals.
suggested_refs: Texas State Historical Association, Handbook of Texas, 'La Reunion'

stops.name: Guise, the Familistere
stops.date_confidence: French Wikipedia dates Godin's discovery of Fourier to 1842 and construction from 1858 to 1859, continuing into the 1880s; the Societe du Familistere is dated 1880, the Monument Historique classification 4 July 1991, and Musee de France status from 2010. Month and day of the start of building are unrecorded and defaulted. The research pool carries two longitudes for the site, 3.6247 and 3.6253; the first is used and the divergence recorded.
stops.campa: Jean-Baptiste Andre Godin, an ironfounder who read Fourier in 1842, builds his own version at Guise from 1858: the Familistere, a social palace of glazed courtyards, apartments, schools, baths and a theatre for the workers of his stove foundry. He keeps the building and drops the passionate series. It is the most durable thing the phalanstery ever became. In 1880 he converts the whole enterprise into a producers' cooperative; it is classed a historic monument on 4 July 1991 and has been a museum since 2010.

stops.name: Boulevard de Clichy, the bronze
stops.date_confidence: French Wikipedia gives the Derre bronze, funded by public subscription, inaugurated June 1899 by the disciple Jean-Adolphe Alhaiza; the day is not given. Coordinates follow the boulevard de Clichy article, which places the pedestal on the central island at the level of the lycee Jules-Ferry. The research pool's two lenses disagree with each other here, 2.3281 against 2.3325, the latter being the place Blanche longitude some 300 metres east; the disagreement is recorded and not averaged.
stops.campa: Sixty-two years after his death Paris puts him on a pedestal. Emile Derre's bronze, paid for by public subscription, is inaugurated in June 1899 on the central island of the boulevard de Clichy by the lycee Jules-Ferry, and unveiled by the disciple Jean-Adolphe Alhaiza. The Third Republic claims a thinker it had no use for while he lived. The pedestal stands in a quarter of theatres and dance halls, a few streets from the cemetery where he is buried.

stops.name: Boulevard de Clichy, the metal drive
stops.date_confidence: French Wikipedia records the melting of the statue for metal by the occupying authorities under Vichy, without giving a year within the Occupation; the research pool brackets it 1941 to 1944 and 1942 is a placeholder inside that. The Breton detail is dated 1945 for the American West journey and 1947 for the publication of the Ode, both attested by French Wikipedia's Breton article and English Wikipedia's works list.
stops.campa: The bronze is taken down and melted for metal under the Occupation, one of a great many Paris statues to go the same way. The requisition runs under Vichy from 1941, and no source reached records the year this one went. What remains on the terre-plein is the stone pedestal with his name cut into it and nothing standing above. In 1945 Andre Breton carries volumes of Fourier across the American West, and in 1947 he publishes the Ode a Charles Fourier.
suggested_refs: Andre Breton, Ode a Charles Fourier (1947)
Herbert Marcuse, Eros and Civilization (1955), on Fourier and non-repressive sublimation

stops.name: Besancon, the plaque on a street cut after him
stops.date_confidence: The plaque is attested by French Wikipedia's article on the rue Moncey, which quotes it: au n. 2, plaque commemorant le lieu de naissance du philosophe Charles Fourier (1772-1837). No date of installation is recorded anywhere reached, and the pool says only twentieth century; 1950 is an arbitrary placeholder used to order the segment. Coordinates corrected to the article's own geolocation of the street, about 120 metres from the pool's value.
stops.campa: At number 2 rue Moncey in Besancon a plaque marks the birthplace of the philosopher Charles Fourier, 1772 to 1837. It gives the two dates and the word philosophe, and says nothing about cloth. The street it is fixed to did not exist when he was born: the rue Moncey was cut through in 1836 to 1838, replacing the medieval ruelle Baron at whose corner the drapery stood, and the work began while he was still alive and writing in Paris. Nobody records the year the plaque went up.

stops.name: Paris, the manuscript printed at last
stops.date_confidence: The 1967 Debout edition is attested by English Wikipedia; her L'Utopie de Charles Fourier is dated 1978 by French Wikipedia. Month and day unrecorded and defaulted. Coordinates are the corpus canonical Paris pin, standing for the publication rather than a located address. Barthes's Sade, Fourier, Loyola is dated 1971.
stops.campa: Simone Debout edits and publishes Le Nouveau Monde amoureux, a hundred and fifty years after it was written and a hundred and thirty after its author died. The manuscript on marriage, divorce, sexual pluralism and desire between people of the same sex enters print in the decade that was ready for it. Fourier stops being a footnote in the history of socialism and becomes a writer. Four years later Roland Barthes puts him beside Sade and Loyola, in a book named for the three of them.
suggested_refs: Simone Debout, L'Utopie de Charles Fourier (1978)

stops.name: Boulevard de Clichy, the plaster copy
stops.date_confidence: Attested to the day by French Wikipedia, which credits libertarian and situationist groups and records that the copy was removed within days. The research pool placed this during a period of general strike, which is wrong: the general strike was May and June 1968, ten months earlier.
stops.campa: On 10 March 1969 a plaster copy of Derre's melted bronze appears overnight on the empty pedestal, put there by libertarian and situationist groups. The gesture belongs to the aftermath of May 1968, when a generation that had rediscovered attractive labour and the critique of everyday life went looking for ancestors and found the place where one had stood until the metal drive. The plaster keeps the pedestal for a few days, and then it is taken away.

stops.name: Boulevard de Clichy, the fourth apple
stops.date_confidence: French Wikipedia dates Franck Scurti's La Quatrieme Pomme to 2011 on the same pedestal; month and day unrecorded and defaulted. Fourier's apple anecdote, the Paris restaurant and the price comparison, is his own and is reported in the general biographical record rather than from a dated document.
stops.campa: In 2011 the artist Franck Scurti installs La Quatrieme Pomme on the same pedestal, a fourth apple set beside the three that are said to have changed the world. The pedestal carries the fruit and not the man. The joke is Fourier's own: he told of paying a preposterous price for an apple in a Paris restaurant, the same fruit that cost a hundred times less in the country he had just travelled from, and he dated the whole of his social calculus from that moment.
